title: CI/CD for Kubernetes 🚀
description: Build automated pipelines to continuously deliver applications to your cluster.

slides.title: CI/CD in a Container World 🌍
slides.content:
# From code to cluster, automatically

Continuous Integration (CI) builds and tests your application on every commit.
Continuous Delivery/Deployment (CD) automatically deploys those changes to Kubernetes.

A typical pipeline:
1. Push code → build container image.
2. Run tests (unit, integration).
3. Push image to registry.
4. Update Kubernetes manifests (e.g., change image tag).
5. Apply to cluster.

slides.title: Key Tools 🔧
slides.content:
## Popular CI/CD platforms

- **GitHub Actions** – tightly integrated with GitHub, many pre‑built actions.
- **GitLab CI** – built‑in registry, Kubernetes integration.
- **Jenkins** – powerful but requires more setup.
- **Tekton** – Kubernetes‑native pipeline engine.
- **Argo Workflows/Events** – for complex event‑driven workflows.

All can build, test, and deploy to Kubernetes using kubectl or Helm commands.

slides.title: Example: GitHub Actions Pipeline ⚡
slides.content:
## Build, test, deploy

```yaml
name: Build and Deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  build-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Build container
        run: docker build -t myapp:${{ github.sha }} .
      - name: Push to registry
        run: |
          docker tag myapp:${{ github.sha }} myregistry/myapp:${{ github.sha }}
          docker push myregistry/myapp:${{ github.sha }}
      - name: Set image in manifests
        run: |
          sed -i "s|image:.*|image: myregistry/myapp:${{ github.sha }}|" k8s/deployment.yaml
      - name: Deploy to cluster
        uses: appleboy/kubectl-action@master
        with:
          kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}
          args: apply -f k8s/
```

quizData.question: Why is it common to use `${{ github.sha }}` as an image tag?

options.text: It's the fastest tag to type
It provides a unique, immutable tag for each build

quizData.explanation: Commit SHA ensures each image version is uniquely identifiable and traceable to code.

slides.title: Updating Manifests: The 'Write Back' Pattern ↩️
slides.content:
## Keep your Git repo in sync

Instead of just applying a change, update the YAML file in Git (e.g., via a PR) and let the CD tool merge and apply. This is the basis of **GitOps**.

Tools like **Renovate** or **Argo CD Image Updater** can automatically open PRs to update image tags.

slides.title: Securing Deployments 🔐
slides.content:
## Never hard‑code credentials

- Use Kubernetes Secrets or external secret stores.
- Inject registry credentials via `imagePullSecrets`.
- Use short‑lived tokens for pipeline access (e.g., OIDC with GitHub Actions).
- Limit the pipeline’s RBAC permissions (don't give cluster‑admin).

slides.title: Tokenless Authentication (OIDC)
slides.content: GitHub Actions can authenticate to cloud providers without static secrets:
slides.codeSnippet:
- name: Authenticate to GKE
  uses: google-github-actions/auth@v1
  with:
    workload_identity_provider: 'projects/...'
    service_account: 'my-sa@...'

quizData.question: What is the benefit of using OIDC for GitHub Actions instead of a static KUBECONFIG secret?

options.text: No long‑lived secrets to manage or rotate
It doesn't need a cluster at all

quizData.explanation: OIDC issues short‑lived tokens, eliminating static credential storage.

slides.title: Canary and Blue‑Green Deployments 🐤🔵🟢
slides.content:
## Beyond 'kubectl apply'

Advanced deployment strategies:
- **Rolling update** (default) – gradual replacement.
- **Canary** – shift a small percentage of traffic to new version (via Ingress annotations).
- **Blue‑Green** – deploy a completely new environment and switch traffic (via Service selectors).

These minimize risk during releases.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Use Helm in CI/CD

`helm upgrade --install --atomic --set image.tag=$NEW_TAG` makes rollbacks easy and keeps releases tidy.
